parties:
Abani Mohan Saha ------ Appellant 
Vs.
Assistant Custodian (S.D.O.) Vested Property, Chandpur and ors ------Respondents.
full_judgment:
2. Facts are simple. Plaintiff is the appellant. He filed the suit being Title Suit No. 264 of 1977 in the Court of Munsif, Chandpur, for a declaration that the proceeding of B.P. Case No. 255 of 1972-73 was illegal, void and collusive and for an order directing defendants 3-5 to deliver him possession of the suit property. He claimed the suit property on the basis of a registered deed of gift dated 26-6-1969 from the sons of Surendra Chandra Saha, who was admittedly owner of that property. Defendant No. 2 and father of defendant Nos. 4 and 5 took the lease of the two rooms of the suit premises by a registered kabuliyat dated 10.3.1970. That defendant No.2 handed over possession to defendant No. 3 without any authority. Later defendants 3-5 took settlement from defendant No. 1, the Assistant Custodian. who treated the property as enemy property on the basis of a false report of the Tahsildar. 

 4. Leave was granted to consider the question whether the suit property could be treated as enemy property in view of the deed of gift dated 29.6.69 and the kabuliyat dated 10.3.70. 

 5. The Courts below concurrently found that defendants 4-5 have been in possession of the suit premises since last 30 years back as the bharatia of the original owner of Surendra. This much is admitted that the defendants executed a kabuliyat in 1970 in favour of the plaintiff. This is a registered document. The plaintiff claimed that the three sons of Surendra gifted the property by a registered document dated 23.6.69. At the trial the plaintiff produced the certified copy as the registered deed of gift was burnt during the liberation war. 

 6. The trial court came to the conclusion that the plaintiff cannot claim the property on the basis of the alleged deed of gift Ext. 1, inasmuch as, "the alleged executants made contradictory statements in respect of their very possession" and further the plaintiff failed to produce "vital and harmonious evidence with regard to the circumstances of the preparation of the gift deed." Next it was considered that the plaintiff did not mention that the original deed was burnt in his pleadings. As for the kabuliyat Exts, 2 and 2(a) the trial Court took the view "the kabuliyat dated 9-3-70 cannot support the plaintiff to the effect that Khalil Pathan and K. Rahman took bhara of the suit property in 1970". Then significantly adds "although it is apparently to that effect". 

 10. Neither the sons of Surendra had come forward to challenge it nor any other heirs of Surendra questioned the document. It is being questioned by certain interested persons, namely. defendants 3 to 5, who were the bharatias of Surendra for last 30 years or so and who in 1970 immediately after the deed of gift executed kabuliyat in favour of the plaintiff. These persons made an about turn in their own interest and the easiest thing for them was to move the Assistant Custodian of Enemy Property for treating as enemy property and ultimately got settlement in fact from him. This is what has happened in this case. The deed of gift was registered in 1969. These bharatias defendants 3 to 5 executed their kabuliyats in 1970 in favour of the plaintiff, and they are estopped from denying the title of the plaintiff This circumstance is enough to prove the title of the plaintiff. 

 M. H. Rahman, J.- The appellant instituted Title Suit No. 264 of 1977 in the Second Court of Munsif, Chandpur for a declaration that the proceeding of E. P. Case No. 255 of 1972-73 was illegal, void and collusive and for an order directing defendants Nos. 3-5 to deliver him possession of the suit-property. He claimed the suit property on the basis of a registered deed of gift dated 26th June, 1969 from the three sons of Surendra Chandra Saha, who was admittedly the original owner of that properly. His further case is that defendant No. 2 and the father of defendant Nos. 4 and 5 took lease of two rooms of the suit premises by registered kabuliyats dated 10th March, 1970 and they had been carrying on business there; that subsequently defendant No. 2 illegally handed over possession to defendant No. 3; that after a local arbitration in the matter defendant Nos. 3-5, though agreed to deliver up possession they did not do so and instead, they took settlement from defendant No. 1, the Assistant Custodian ( S.D.O.) of the vested properties. Chandpur who illegally treated the suit property as enemy property on the basis of a false report of the local Tahsildar. 

 On behalf of the appellant it is contended that in view of the registered deed of gift, Ext. 1. and the evidence of P. W. 1 that the executants of the gift left for India in 1971 during the liberation war and as there was no evidence to show that the executant of the deed of gift were residing in India since 1965 the courts below erred in law in not accepting the plaintiff's case. It is further contended that the deed of gift is a registered document, and as its registration in the manner provided by the Registration Act was not disputed that document ought not to have been rejected as the substantive evidence of the plaintiff's title to the suit-land, particularly when defendant No. 2 Khalil Pathan and Khalilur Rahman the father of defendant Nos. 4 and 5, executed registered kabuliyats in 1970 in favour of the plaintiff. 

 30. When the plaintiff failed to prove his title to the suit premises his claim that he was in possession of the premises through the lessees who executed the Kabuliyats in 1970 calls for closer scrutiny. Instead of the executants, P.W. 3 Dhirendra the scribe, came to depose with regard to the execution of the kabuliyats, P.W. 3 could not say who identified the executants. He stated that Majib Hazi and Narendra Mohan Saba were witnesses to the kabuliyats, Majib was well and alive but he was not examined. P.W. 4 Narendra Mohan Saba who knew the plaintiff and the suit house asserted that be was an attesting witness in the kabuliyats. He could not, however, say when Nityananda, one of the executants of the deed, possessed the suit house. He could not say even by guess when Nityananda last possessed the suit house. Even if the kabuliyats are accepted as genuine documents they could not support the plaintiff's claim of title to the suit land when his basic document was disbelieved by all the Courts below. The evidence of P. W. 2 lends support to the contention of defendant Nos. 4 and 5 that they and their predecessors had been in the premises for thirty years as tenants of Surendra, the original owner.
